column1: Why do low-register orchestral sections (basses, cellos) require more players than violins to balance?
column2: Fletcher-Munson equal-loudness curves show the ear is far less sensitive to bass frequencies — a 100 Hz tone needs ~10 dB more acoustic energy than a 1000 Hz tone to sound equally loud, so low strings need greater numbers (and often doubling with bassoon/contrabassoon) to register as equally present.

column1: What is the spacing rule of thumb for voicing a chord from bottom to top in an orchestra?
column2: Space the bottom of the chord by a 5th or more (and often octaves/12ths); keep the top of the chord closer, by a 3rd or less. This prevents low-register mud while allowing clear close harmony up high.

column1: Why does a tight low triad (e.g., C2-E2-G2) sound muddy while the same notes spread across octaves (C2-G2-E3-C4) sound clear?
column2: The ear's critical bands are roughly constant in Hz (~100-160 Hz wide) regardless of pitch, so at low frequencies a narrow interval crams multiple fundamentals and overlapping harmonics into one band, causing beating/masking ('mud'). Spreading the notes moves each fundamental's harmonics into separate critical bands, clearing the mix.

column1: What does spectral masking imply for scoring a quiet solo instrument (e.g., oboe) against loud dense brass?
column2: A loud, spectrally dense sound (full brass) will bury a quiet, spectrally sparse one sharing its frequency range even with a 'reasonable' dynamic gap — there is no middle ground where a lone soft instrument survives against ff brass; it must be given thin accompaniment or the brass must thin out/double it in unison.

column1: In full orchestral score layout, what is the standard top-to-bottom section order?
column2: Woodwinds → Brass → Percussion → Harp/Keyboard/Voice (if present) → Strings.

column1: Within the woodwind block of a full score, what is the standard top-to-bottom instrument order?
column2: Piccolo → Flute 1,2 → Oboe 1,2 → English Horn → Clarinet 1,2 → Bass Clarinet → Bassoon 1,2 → Contrabassoon.

column1: Within the string section of a full score, what is the standard top-to-bottom order?
column2: Violin I → Violin II → Viola → Cello → Double Bass.

column1: Why does a dynamic marking like 'f' not correspond to a fixed physical intensity across instruments or sections?
column2: Dynamics are relative, not absolute: a marking tells a player to produce roughly a given fraction of their instrument's usable dynamic range, judged against everyone else playing at that moment. A solo trombone f and a tutti string section f are different physical intensities aimed at the same perceptual balance.

column1: What harmonic content does a clarinet (cylindrical bore, closed at the reed end) produce, and what timbral effect results?
column2: It produces mostly odd harmonics, giving a hollow, covered sound, especially pronounced in the low chalumeau register.

column1: Why does doubling flute and clarinet at the unison often sound thin and hollow rather than full?
column2: Both instruments have spectra missing significant harmonic content (flute: full series but weak upper partials; clarinet: mostly odd harmonics only), so combining them adds two incomplete spectra together rather than filling in each other's gaps — a known orchestration trap.

column1: According to the critical band rule for harmony, what interval/frequency condition causes audible beating ('roughness') between two pitches?
column2: Any two sounding pitches within roughly a minor third of each other, when both are below about 200 Hz, will have overtones close enough together to beat audibly — this is why low, close chords sound muddy and wide low chords sound clean.

column1: Why does doubling two violins playing the identical written pitch make the sound 'bigger' rather than 'flangier', while pitch-shifting a single sampled line a few cents sounds synthetic?
column2: Real players have independent natural pitch spread (±5–10 cents) and non-locked vibrato (5–7 Hz) while their attack transients (bow catching the string) still align within milliseconds — constructive widening without losing the attack. A pitch-shifted copy has no independent vibrato, so it lacks this natural, uncorrelated modulation.
